impressions: Metastatic lesions described in the bilateral cerebral hemispheres and posteroinferior right caudate nucleus,

Metastatic solid lesions described at the level of the left cerebellar hemisphere and left cerebellar tonsil, due to the edema compression around the left cerebellar hemisphere and the metastatic solid lesion present in the left cerebellar tonsil, the cerebral aqueduct and foramen of Magendie (central canal posteriorly) appear nearly occluded. findings: Multiple metastatic lesions were observed in the bilateral cerebral hemispheres, the largest measuring 27x25 mm in the anterior left frontal lobe, located subcortically and cortically, isohyperintense on T2-weighted series, hypointense on T1-weighted series, showing heterogeneous intense contrast enhancement on post-contrast series, with surrounding edema signals observed. Hypointensities related to hemorrhage were observed in some of the described metastatic lesions on the SWI sequence.

A solid metastatic lesion of the same character was observed involving the posteroinferior portion of the right caudate nucleus, causing mild compression on the 3rd ventricle, and causing compression on the right Foramen of Monro.

Two solid metastatic lesions of the same character were observed posteriorly at the level of the middle cerebellar peduncle, in the left cerebellar hemisphere posterolaterally and immediately anterior to it, the largest measuring 41x37 mm. Significant edema signal is present around the described metastatic lesions in the left cerebellum; the edema has caused significant compression on the cerebral aqueduct and has nearly occluded it, and appears to significantly narrow the 4th ventricle by causing compression. Accordingly, dilation is present in the 3rd ventricle and bilateral lateral ventricles. Edema signal increases associated with transependymal flow were observed around the bilateral lateral ventricles. Findings should be evaluated clinically in the context of obstructive hydrocephalus.

A solid metastatic lesion of the same character measuring 13x9 mm was observed inferiorly at the level of the left cerebellar tonsil. Due to the edema signals of the two lesions described in the left cerebellar hemisphere and the lesion present in the left cerebellar tonsil, there is caudal herniation of approximately 1 cm at the level of the cerebellar tonsil, and the central canal appears nearly occluded at this level posteriorly.

findings: In evaluation of infratentorial structures; No pathological signal was detected in the medulla oblongata. Cerebellar fissures and folia appear normal. The cerebellar tonsils show minimal ectopic extension towards the spinal canal from the foramen magnum of approximately 2.5 mm. Hemiatrophic change observed in the right half of the brainstem is consistent with Wallerian degeneration.

In evaluation of the ventricular system and cisterns; Basal cisterns are of normal width; no space-occupying lesion is seen in the cisterns. The cerebellopontine angle cisterns are symmetric and observed at normal width. The 4th ventricle is midline and of normal width. The 3rd ventricle appears normal.

In evaluation of supratentorial structures; Bilateral cortical gray matter, bilateral basal ganglia, bilateral thalami, internal and external capsules, corona radiata, centrum semiovale have normal signal intensity characteristics. Several millimeter-sized nonspecific plaques were detected in the subcortical white matter and deep white matter of both cerebral hemispheres. findings: Upon comparison and evaluation of the patient's examinations:
Previously seen punctate contrast-enhancing micronodules located in the depths of the cerebellar folia persist. Peripheral edema or diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement is not present.

The patient's striking findings are an increase in lesions located in the basal ganglia and thalami. These lesions are signal increases extending along penetrating vessels and are micronodular lesions in places (FLAIR sagittal 126, axial 77; post-Gd sagittal 62, axial 94). This pattern, atypical for neoplastic invasion, suggests fungal infections including Cryptococci causing basal meningitis. Typical gelatinous cysts for Cryptococci are not present; however, both pial-arachnoidal and perivascular micronodules may be of the same etiology.

Micronodular enhancements observed in the depths of the sulci in the anterior and middle cranial fossae persist (post-Gd axial 52, 58, 90, 102, 104). There are no T2 or diffusion correlates for these lesions.
Hydrocephalus, ventriculitis, or parenchymal lesion is not present.

Paranasal sinuses and middle ear cavity are normal.

findings: Upon comparison and evaluation of the patient's examinations;

The 2.5 cm metastasis with solid and cystic components located in the left superior temporal gyrus, identified on the MRI dated [date_1], has transformed into a 1.5 x 1 cm diameter sequela cyst on [date_2], which is non-enhancing, has lost its round shape, and edema has resolved.

impressions: Mass lesion with epicenter in the tectum-pineal region, appearing infiltrative into the mesencephalic-pontine tegmentum and bilateral medial thalamus, composed of solid-cystic components, compressing the fourth ventricle, obliterating the pineal cistern, and pushing the third ventricle anteriorly and cerebellar vermis posteriorly.

Solid nodular lesion compatible with seeding metastasis on the wall of the left lateral ventricle frontal horn (The examination was obtained without contrast. Control MRI examinations are recommended to be performed with contrast).

findings: The examination was evaluated considering the previous CSF flow MRI examination dated [date_1] available in the radiology image archive system.

There is a mass with epicenter in the mesencephalic tectum-pineal region, appearing infiltrative into the mesencephalic-pontine tegmentum and bilateral medial thalamus, composed of solid-cystic components, with signals compatible with millimetric hemorrhage-calcification observed within the solid components. In the current examination, the mass dimensions were measured as 68 mm in the anterior-posterior axis at the widest point, 62 mm in the laterolateral axis in the axial plane, and 64 mm in the craniocaudal axis in the sagittal plane. When comparing the sagittal T2-weighted images directed towards the midline in the previous examination with the sagittal images in the current examination, it is observed that in the current examination, a proteinaceous cystic component with prominent expansile lobulated contours and thin septa is seen superior to the mass, and consequently, the third ventricle is significantly compressed from posteriorly up to the level of the foramen of Monro, the thalami are pushed towards the lateral side, and the solid component of the mass is pushed into the fourth ventricle and towards the cerebellar vermis. As far as can be evaluated on sagittal images, no obvious dimensional increase is identified in the solid component. In the current examination, nearly the entirety of the fourth ventricle appears obliterated. The dimensions of the cystic component defined superior to the mass were measured as 58 mm in the anterior-posterior axis, 32 mm in the laterolateral axis, and 26 mm in the craniocaudal axis. Compensatory dilation is observed in the third ventricle and lateral ventricles pushed anteriorly (Third ventricle transverse diameter 14 mm, anterior horn diameters of lateral ventricles measured 22 mm on the right and left). A nodular lesion protruding into the ventricle, measured 12x10 mm in size in the axial plane, is observed on the inferolateral wall of the left lateral ventricle frontal horn, which is consistent with seeding metastasis. On sagittal T2-weighted images, a vertical signal void due to CSF flow is visible at the level of the third ventriculostomy, and the third ventriculostomy is evaluated as patent. The corpus callosum is slightly bulging toward the vertex. The corpus section is of thin caliber. Signal is normal. A linear gliosis line following the tract of the third ventriculostomy procedure has been observed in the right frontal lobe. No pathology is detected in other supra-infratentorial neural parenchyma apart from the findings described. No signal change compatible with intracranial acute hemorrhage is observed. No signal change compatible with acute ischemia is detected on diffusion-weighted images.

Both orbits, optic nerves, chiasm, and optic tracts appear normal. A mucous retention cyst is observed in the left maxillary sinus. findings: Brainstem and cerebellum, fourth ventricle, and posterior fossa cisterns are normal.

Starting from the right parietal subcortical area, extending to the ependymal surface, there is a 5 x 4.5 x 4 cm tumefactive plaque with cystic degeneration in the lateral segments. Diffusion restriction is present in the acute inflamed walls of the plaque, and there is contrast enhancement in an “open ring” shape on the ependymal and cortical surfaces. Linear enhancements within the cystic degeneration areas are from inflamed veins. There is minimal edema localized around the plaque, disproportionate to its size.

There is a 2nd lesion of the same characteristics, centrally located in the left central periventricular area, extending to the insular subcortical area, internal and external capsule, lentiform nuclei, and medial thalamus, with edema. The contrast-enhanced segment is 2.5 cm in diameter, and with its edematous peripheral component, it measures 5 x 5 x 4 cm.

Common features of both lesions are their centralization in the white matter, diffusion restriction in the acute inflamed demarcation lines, and contrast enhancement localized only to these areas, along with the disappearance of contrast enhancement in ependymal contact areas. These findings are compatible with tumefactive demyelinating plaques.
No similar or other chronic demyelinating area was detected in other sections of the neural parenchyma, in the corpus callosum and optic nerves, or in the proximal spinal cord.

Pineal gland measures 20 x 13 x 17 mm and is pushing the posterior wall of the 3rd ventricle anteriorly. The gland's size is caused by a pineal cyst. The normal gland is thinned inferiorly and on the left, located in a crescent shape within the pineal calcification, unfragmented, within the solid portion. impressions: Tetraventricular obstructive hydrocephalus with added acute pressure increase; entrapped 4th ventricle.
The presence of adhesions and septa-web in the 4th ventricle outlets, aqueduct, and left lateral ventricle suggests that the chronic hydrocephalus is secondary to prior meningitis or SAH.
The absence of ependymal or leptomeningeal mass or pathological enhancement rules out acute infection – hemorrhage.
findings: There is tetraventricular obstructive hydrocephalus in this patient: Adhesions are present at the Foramen of Magendie, the right Foramen of Luschka where the cistern protrudes, and the Aqueduct of Sylvius, and the 4th ventricle is markedly enlarged. Entrapped 4th ventricle walls show CSF diapedesis and edema, and the brainstem and cerebellum are compressed; posterior fossa cisterns are occluded.
Although the Aqueduct of Sylvius appears widened, the presence of a retraction extending posteriorly from the brainstem on sagittal sections suggests the possibility of a web.

There is pressure hydrocephalus in the 3rd and lateral ventricles. In the left lateral ventricle, ependymal-choroid plexus adhesions and septation at the posterior aspect of the corpus callosum have caused further enlargement in the left atrium-occipital-temporal horns. The thickness of the left anterior temporal parenchyma has decreased to 2 mm. The bilateral Foramina of Monro are markedly wide.
Periventricular edema has developed due to increased pressure, and all cerebral sulci and cisterns have narrowed.
The floor of the 3rd ventricle has bulged downward. Due to motion artifacts, the distance of the free floor and the relationship with the basilar apex-mamillary bodies cannot be stated.
The absence of ventricular or leptomeningeal enhancement, and the lack of evidence of prior SAH on SWI, rule out acute hydrocephalus.
The 4th ventricle outlets, aqueduct, and septation and adhesions in the left lateral ventricle suggest late complications of arachnoiditis and possibly meningitis secondary to a prior event.
Brainstem, cerebral, and cerebellar parenchymal signals are normal except for periventricular edema.
Except for increased perioptic CSF spaces, the extracranial areas are normal.

impressions: Probable high-grade glial tumor involving the left frontal lobe, perisylvian area, insular cortex, and basal ganglia, crossing to the contralateral hemisphere via the corpus callosum, diffuse infiltrative type, containing areas with higher cellularity showing contrast uptake and diffusion restriction.
findings: Left pterional craniotomy defects are observed. In the left hemisphere, a diffuse infiltrative type mass is observed that cannot be clearly distinguished from the infiltrative edema caused by it. This mass is the most prominent appearance, formed in the inferior frontal and perisylvian localization, spreading to the superior middle and inferior frontal gyri, the left insular cortex, and basal ganglia, crossing to the contralateral hemisphere via the corpus callosum genu, involving the left corticospinal tract, and spreading to the vicinity of the left lateral ventricle temporal horn. Following surgery performed on the mass in the inferior frontal gyrus, a resection cavity is observed. In the superior anterior vicinity of the cavity, in the component within the superior frontal gyrus, contrast enhancement is present containing areas of higher grade that show contrast uptake measuring approximately 2x2 cm, and diffusion restriction is observed in this area. In addition, faint contrast enhancements are present in the periventricular localization. A sequela microhemorrhagic focus is present immediately adjacent to the resection cavity. Due to the mass and edema effect, minimal compression is observed in the left lateral ventricle, and a 6 mm rightward shift is observed in the midline structures.

In the right periventricular localization, probable infiltrative edema showing extension to the lateral portions of the basal ganglia and the temporal lobe white matter is observed, which is T2 hyperintense.
The head of the left caudate nucleus, the body portion of the right caudate nucleus, the hypothalamus, and the proximal portions of the bilateral optic tracts remain within the infiltrative edema.
The medulla oblongata and cerebellar hemispheres appear normal.

The main cerebral vascular structures are of narrow caliber but patent.
